messages.content: how to bounce back from a layoff

message.content:
Bouncing back from a layoff works best when you treat it as both an *emotional reset* and a *career project*: first stabilize yourself, then rebuild momentum with a clear plan. Practical steps that show up consistently in career guidance are to take time to process the loss, inventory your strengths, lean on your network or a mentor, stay active through volunteer or freelance work, and use the pause to learn a new skill or credential.[4][2][1]

- **Take a short pause to process it.** Career guidance from Stanford magazine recommends taking time to grieve before launching into the job search, so you can recover enough to make good decisions.[4]
- **Do a skills inventory.** Write down your key achievements, strongest skills, and recent impact so you can explain your value clearly to employers.[2][1]
- **Use your network early.** Reach out to former colleagues, mentors, alumni networks, and professional associations for advice, referrals, and informational interviews.[4][2]
- **Stay active with short-term work.** Volunteering or freelance work helps keep your routine, preserve confidence, and keep your skills current.[2][1]
- **Add a credential or new skill.** A layoff can be a useful time to take an online course or earn a credential in an in-demand area.[2][1]
- **Protect your mental health.** Sources on layoff recovery emphasize exercise, hobbies, walks, meditation, and professional support if stress or shame starts to feel overwhelming.[2][1]

A useful mindset shift is to treat the layoff as a signal to reassess direction, not as a verdict on your ability; one layoff-focused talk explicitly recommends reframing the event as a setback rather than the end of the road.[3]

If you want, I can turn this into a **30-day bounce-back plan** or a **layoff recovery checklist** you can use immediately.
